headline: AI agents successfully decompile 80% of a first-person shooter after 500 billion tokens
summary: A team orchestrated various AI models including Claude and Codex over three months to reconstruct a popular FPS game into C++, achieving a functional main menu and map loading.
details: Over three months and 500 billion tokens, a team of AI agents successfully decompiled approximately 80% of a popular first-person shooter game. The ambitious project aimed to create an accurate, stable, and feature-complete C++ recreation of the original game, complete with security and bug fixes.

The project focused on orchestrating autonomous AI agents, utilizing models like Claude Max, Codex Pro, Sonnet, Opus, Luna, Sol, and Terra. Agents managed GitHub issues for progress tracking and communicated via Discord, with a webhook notifying them of CI failures.

The setup involved three worker agents for decompiling and committing code, alongside one reviewer agent coordinating and flagging bugs. They primarily used Hex-Rays' ida-mcp for its stability and headless operation, crucial for automated decompilation.

Key challenges included agents losing focus over time and managing context efficiently. To combat this, the team implemented earlier context compactions (at 42% fill) to remove irrelevant information and an hourly cron job to inject a document defining goals and work protocols.

Despite the complexities, the agents achieved significant progress, enabling the game to launch, display its main menu, and load maps. This project served as a deep dive into effective AI orchestration over extended periods, showcasing the potential for autonomous development.

headline_marked: [[How much RAM you actually need]] to run AI locally
headline: How much RAM you actually need to run AI locally
summary: Forget core counts and price tags. The real determinant for running AI locally is unified memory, specifically how much is available after the OS takes its share. This guide breaks down the practical RAM requirements.
details: Higher-end AI PCs range from $2,599 to $5,999, but their core count or price isn't the primary factor for local AI. Instead, the amount of unified memory available to the model, after the operating system's allocation, is what truly determines capability.

For example, a 128 GB machine might only report around 110 GB of GPU-addressable memory, with the OS consuming the rest. This means the full advertised RAM is not entirely available for AI model weights and context.

Practically, 24 GB becomes tight quickly once the operating system takes its share, limiting model size. Configurations with 64 GB and 128 GB are essential for running larger models like 70B, making a significant difference in capability.

The article advises choosing your desired AI model first, then determining the necessary memory, and finally comparing prices. This approach often leads to a more cost-effective and capable setup, avoiding overspending on cores without sufficient RAM.
